catalog_quote: Der Ton ruht im Jakutischen, so viel ich habe bemerken können, immer auf der Endsilbe des Wortes.

new_statements.quote: 2.3.1 Word accent. Sakha has a stress-accent system, which does not have a distinctive function. The final syllable of a word is regularly accented. The stress does not fall in the final syllable of a few exceptional words, which originate from compounding words. Stressed vowels are usually in high pitch and only sometimes in extremely low pitch with preaching or teasing nuances. 2.3.2 Phrasal accent. Quite simply, while the accent of the former element(s) in a phrase is kept steady, that of the last element becomes less stressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (StressTyp2 final-syllable rule); adds that stress is non-contrastive, that a few lexicalized compounds are exceptions, the pitch realization, and the phrasal-accent behaviour. Custody note: the listed open_url (the Harvard library catalogue) resolves to a different work, Ebata 2024 'Passive and Reflexive Voices in Sakha (Yakut) and Tyvan', Altai Hakpo 34:149-158 (wrong item, saved); the 2011 sketch was downloaded instead from the the Internet Archive copy of the original ILCAA volume PDF (lingdy.aacore.jp/jp/material/, 2016-03-03 capture). text of the volume drops 'ch'/'Th' ligatures, so the page was re-scanned for the quote.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-distinctive stress accent on the last syllable of every word; realized mainly as high pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Phrasal level: earlier elements of a phrase keep their accent, the last element is weakened.
new_statements.exceptions: A few words that originate from compounds do not have final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Ebata 2011 describes present-day Sakha of the Sakha Republic (no dialect named); Böhtlingk 1851 describes mid-19th-century Yakut from Uwarowskij's texts and Middendorff's notes, likewise without dialect specification. No work describes Dolgan or another variety.

new_statements.quote: Betonung. Der Ton ruht im Jakutischen, so viel ich habe bemerken können, immer auf der Endsilbe des Wortes. So ist es auch Middendorff vorgekommen, wie man auch aus seinen Papieren ersehen kann. Nach Herrn Ogorodnikow ruht der Ton meist auf der letzten Silbe. Letzterer verwechselt übrigens den langen Vocal mit dem betonten, da er einigen Wörtern einen zweifachen Ton beilegt. [p. 151] — Längen und Diphthonge werden, wie man sieht, durch einen Acut, der Wortaccent durch einen Gravis über dem letzten Bestandtheil der Endsilbe bezeichnet [Einleitung, on Dawydow's transcription of a Yakut text]
new_statements.translation: Stress. In Yakut the stress rests, as far as I have been able to observe, always on the final syllable of the word. Middendorff found the same, as can also be seen from his papers. According to Mr Ogorodnikov the stress rests mostly on the last syllable. The latter, incidentally, confuses the long vowel with the stressed one, since he assigns a double stress to some words. — Long vowels and diphthongs are, as one sees, marked with an acute, the word accent with a grave over the last component of the final syllable.

sources.note: First instrumental study of Yakut word prosody: treats Yakut as a non-tonal quantity language with regular word-final stress (citing Anderson 1998); f0 maxima and f0 slope differ between short and long vowels, so pitch is a secondary correlate of vowel quantity; the f0 quantity effect appears only in the first (unstressed) syllable, not in the stressed final syllable, which the authors liken to Finnish ('f0 distinctions between quantities appearing only on syllables that have tonal targets', i.e. intonational targets, not lexical tone).
